newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: TEN CATE SEES ASIAN EXPANSION AHEAD.
newsitem.headline: TEN CATE SEES ASIAN EXPANSION AHEAD.

text.p: Textiles and plastics firm Koninklijke Ten Cate NV said on Tuesday it would seek further growth in 1997 with South-East Asia as one of its focus areas.

"Asia is very important for us and we will buy some company there this year or start something with another partner. We want to be in that market," management board member Hans van de Sande told a news conference on Ten Cate's 1996 annual report.

Ten Cate is already active in Malaysia and Singapore where it generates five percent of group turnover. The company will start local production in other Asian countries when its market position is big enough in those areas.
Chairman Frank Schreve said 1997 would be a transition year for Ten Cate after a number of years in which the company has raised profitability.

This year, all product groups will be evaluated. Activities with high returns or potential will be expanded, possibly by takeovers, but units which do not meet the profitability demands, show enough prospects or have enough synergy with other activities might be sold.
Schreve said Ten Cate would probably start with takeovers and disinvestments in 1997 but the major part of this process would take place in 1998 and 1999.
In 1996, Ten Cate raised net profit to 30.2 million guilders from 20.5 million in the previous year.
The 1996 figure included a net extraordinary charge of 5.5 million guilders, mainly because of problems at the group's denim division, which was the only loss-making sector in 1996.

The denim group includes 50 percent owned unit Atlantic Mills in Ireland and Greece's Hellenic Fabrics , of which Ten Cate owns 64 percent. The division posted a 1996 operating loss of nine million guilders, compared with an operating profit of one million in 1995.
For 1997 a recovery in this sector is expected but Schreve said the denim group would still be reorganised, although not all problems might be solved by the end of the year.

He said various options were open, varying from selling parts of the division to increasing influence on jointly owned units or teaming up with other partners. He added Ten Cate was in talks with various parties but declined to elaborate.
Schreve also declined comment on press reports that French textiles group DMC , with whom Ten Cate jointly owns Ireland's Atlantic Mills, wants to get rid of its stake in the Irish denim maker.

Reorganising the denim group will cause another one-off charge in 1997 but Schreve said the balance of extraordinary items need not necessarily be negative this year as a result of possible sales. He declined to elaborate.

The chairman said Ten Cate's rubber products division, where operating profits fell by five million guilders to 12 million last year, expected a sound recovery in 1997. This was backed by developments in the first few months of the year, he added.
The specialised textiles and plastics divisions showed good profitability levels and had gained strong market positions, Schreve said.
Ten Cate reiterated it expected a continuing improvement in profitability in 1997 but did not give any forecasts of percentage growth or expected profits.
